blocks.text: Hold your hand beside a glowing electric heater element and you feel its warmth even though no air is moving between you. A steel billet at 900 K cools mostly by the same mechanism, which needs no medium and depends on the fourth power of absolute temperature.

blocks.markdown: **Thermal radiation** is electromagnetic energy emitted by matter because of its temperature. Unlike conduction and convection it needs no medium. Every surface above absolute zero emits, and for engineering temperatures the relevant wavelengths are about 0.1 to 100 $\mu$m (ultraviolet to infrared). We need an ideal reference to measure real surfaces against: the blackbody.

blocks.title: Blackbody
blocks.text: A blackbody absorbs all incident radiation at every wavelength and direction, and it emits the maximum possible radiation at a given temperature. Its total emissive power (W/m$^2$) is given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, $E_b=\sigma T^4$, where $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$K$^4$ and $T$ is the absolute temperature (K).

blocks.caption: Stefan-Boltzmann law (total emissive power of a blackbody) and Wien's displacement law (wavelength of peak emission)

blocks.title: Emissive power of a furnace aperture
blocks.prompt: A small hole in the wall of a well-insulated furnace at 1500 K behaves almost as a blackbody. Find the emissive power of the aperture and the wavelength at which its spectrum peaks. Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$K$^4$ and Wien's constant 2898 $\mu$m K.

steps.text: A blackbody emits the maximum possible radiation at any temperature. Its total emissive power (energy leaving per unit area, over all wavelengths and directions) depends only on the absolute temperature.
Wien's displacement law gives the peak: $\lambda_{max}=2898/1500=1.93$ $\mu$m, which is in the infrared (visible light is about 0.4 to 0.7 $\mu$m).
Interpretation: at this temperature most of the energy is infrared, with a small visible fraction that makes the aperture glow orange.

blocks.markdown: A real surface emits less than a blackbody. The **emissivity** $\varepsilon$ is the ratio of its emissive power to the blackbody value at the same temperature, $E=\varepsilon\sigma T^4$, with $0\le\varepsilon\le1$. When $\varepsilon$ is assumed independent of wavelength the surface is called **gray**. Emissivity depends on material and surface condition (oxidised or polished) and on temperature.

rows: Reference case; cavities with small openings approximate it
Black paint, roughened or oxidised surfaces
blocks.caption: Representative total emissivities near room temperature to a few hundred degrees (typical values)

blocks.markdown: When radiation strikes a surface it is partly **absorbed**, partly **reflected** and partly **transmitted**. Define the fractions of incident radiation: absorptivity $\alpha$, reflectivity $\rho$ and transmissivity $\tau$. Energy conservation, applied to the incident radiation, requires that the three fractions add up to the whole.

blocks.caption: Total (over all wavelengths) radiative properties; for a diffuse gray surface Kirchhoff's law gives alpha = epsilon

blocks.markdown: For an opaque surface, high absorptivity means low reflectivity. Kirchhoff's law states that, for a diffuse gray surface, $\alpha=\varepsilon$: a good emitter is a good absorber. The net radiation exchange of a small gray body of surface area $A$ and temperature $T_s$ with much larger isothermal surroundings at $T_{sur}$ is simple, because all the radiation leaving the body is absorbed by the surroundings and the surroundings' own emissivity is irrelevant.

blocks.caption: Net radiation from a small gray body to large surroundings; T in kelvin; h_r = epsilon sigma (T_s + T_sur)(T_s^2 + T_sur^2)

blocks.title: Radiation from a hot steel plate to a large room
blocks.prompt: A steel plate surface at 400 $^\circ$C with total hemispherical emissivity 0.8 (typical for oxidised steel) is in a large room whose walls are at 300 K. Find the net radiative heat flux from the plate, and the equivalent radiation heat transfer coefficient.

steps.text: The plate is small compared with the room, so the room behaves as a blackbody enclosure at 300 K for the plate. Radiation exchange between a small gray body and large surroundings is $q''=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)$ with temperatures in kelvin.

Equivalent coefficient: $h_r=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s+T_{sur})(T_s^2+T_{sur}^2)=24.0$ W/m$^2$K, so $q''=h_r(T_s-T_{sur})$. This is comparable with or larger than a natural convection coefficient in air, so radiation cannot be ignored for hot surfaces.

blocks.title: Absolute temperatures only
blocks.text: The fourth-power law requires kelvin. Using $^\circ$C gives nonsense, and even a temperature difference does not work: $T_s^4-T_{sur}^4$ is not $(T_s-T_{sur})^4$. Also the formula for a small body inside a large enclosure does not apply when two surfaces of comparable size exchange radiation; then view factors are needed.

blocks.title: Radiation versus convection
blocks.text: Radiation grows as $T^4$ and dominates at high temperature, while it is also significant near room temperature (about 6 W/m$^2$K for $\varepsilon=1$ at 300 K), comparable with natural convection. A low-emissivity surface (polished metal) minimises radiation, and a black surface maximises it.

points: Blackbody emissive power $E_b=\sigma T^4$ ($T$ in K); real surfaces emit $E=\varepsilon\sigma T^4$.
$\alpha+\rho+\tau=1$ and for opaque surfaces $\alpha+\rho=1$; for a diffuse gray surface $\alpha=\varepsilon$.
Small gray body in large surroundings: $q=\varepsilon A\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)$.

questions.stem: A blackbody has its absolute temperature doubled (for example from 400 K to 800 K). Its total emissive power increases by a factor of

distractorRationale.a: This assumes a linear dependence; $E_b\propto T^4$.
distractorRationale.d: This would be $T^3$; the Stefan-Boltzmann law has $T^4$.

questions.explanation: $E_b=\sigma T^4$ so doubling $T$ multiplies it by $2^4=16$. This strong dependence is why radiation dominates at furnace temperatures.

questions.stem: An opaque surface has absorptivity $\alpha=0.65$ for the incident radiation. Its reflectivity is

distractorRationale.b: This would hold only if the surface reflected exactly what it absorbed; it needs $\alpha+\rho=1$.

questions.explanation: For an opaque surface $\tau=0$, so $\alpha+\rho=1$ and $\rho=1-0.65=0.35$. Energy is conserved: the radiation not absorbed is reflected.

questions.stem: An electric heating element behaves as a blackbody at 1100 K. Using $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$K$^4$, find its emissive power in kW/m$^2$.
questions.explanation: $E_b=\sigma T^4=5.67\times10^{-8}\times1100^4=5.67\times10^{-8}\times1.4641e+12=83014$ W/m$^2$ $=83.0$ kW/m$^2$. Temperature must be in kelvin.

questions.stem: An oxidised steel pipe (total emissivity 0.75) has a surface temperature of 350 K and lies in a large room with walls at 290 K. Find the net radiative heat flux from the pipe surface in W/m$^2$. Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$K$^4$.
questions.explanation: $q''=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)=0.75\times5.67\times10^{-8}\times(1.5006e+10-7.0728e+09)=337.4$ W/m$^2$. The room is large, so its emissivity does not matter.

questions.stem: A small sphere of diameter 0.10 m at 400 K with total emissivity 0.6 hangs in a very large room with walls at 300 K. Find the net rate of radiation heat loss from the sphere in W.
A glass sheet in the infrared is partly transparent. For the incident radiation it has absorptivity 0.08 and reflectivity 0.07. Its transmissivity is

distractorRationale.a: This is $\alpha+\rho$, the opaque part of the radiation, not the transmitted fraction.
distractorRationale.b: This is $1-\rho$ (wrongly leaving out the absorbed fraction).
distractorRationale.c: Subtracting the two properties from each other has no physical basis.

questions.explanation: $\alpha+\rho+\tau=1$ gives $\tau=1-0.08-0.07=0.85$. The sum rule applies to any surface, whether opaque or semi-transparent.

questions.stem: A diffuse gray surface has total emissivity 0.20. By Kirchhoff's law, if it is also opaque, the fraction of incident radiation it reflects is

distractorRationale.a: This is the absorptivity; the reflectivity is its complement.
distractorRationale.c: Zero reflectivity would need a blackbody.
distractorRationale.d: This would make absorptivity zero, contradicting $\alpha=\varepsilon=0.2$.

questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's law for a diffuse gray surface gives $\alpha=\varepsilon=0.20$. For an opaque surface $\rho=1-\alpha=0.80$, which is why polished (low-$\varepsilon$) metal is a good reflector.

questions.stem: Define absorptivity, reflectivity and transmissivity of a surface and show from an energy balance on the incident radiation that they sum to one. State the form of this relation for an opaque surface and explain why a polished metal surface is a poor emitter.
markingGuide: Absorptivity $\alpha$, reflectivity $\rho$ and transmissivity $\tau$ are the fractions of incident radiation that are absorbed, reflected and transmitted.
Energy conservation: all the incident radiation must be absorbed, reflected or transmitted, so $\alpha+\rho+\tau=1$.
By Kirchhoff's law a diffuse gray surface has $\varepsilon=\alpha$; polished metal reflects most radiation ($\rho$ high), so $\alpha$ and therefore $\varepsilon$ are low.
questions.explanation: The energy balance argument is the heart of this: incident energy must go somewhere. Kirchhoff's law links the low absorptivity of a reflective surface to a low emissivity.

questions.stem: The net radiation from a small gray body at $T_s$ inside a very large isothermal enclosure at $T_{sur}$ is $q=\varepsilon A\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)$, in which the emissivity of the enclosure does not appear. Explain why, and state the conditions under which this expression is valid.
markingGuide: The enclosure is much larger than the body, so radiation leaving the body strikes the enclosure and almost none that is reflected returns to the body (reflected energy is spread over the large area).
So the enclosure acts as a blackbody at $T_{sur}$ for the body, absorbing everything and emitting $\sigma T_{sur}^4$ onto it.
The body absorbs a fraction $\alpha=\varepsilon$ of this irradiation, giving the $\varepsilon\sigma T_{sur}^4$ term and emits $\varepsilon\sigma T_s^4$.
Conditions: $A_{body}\ll A_{enclosure}$ (or enclosure nearly black), gray diffuse body with $\alpha=\varepsilon$, isothermal surroundings, temperatures in kelvin.
questions.explanation: The key assumption is the area ratio, which makes the enclosure's reflection negligible. In the radiation network the enclosure's surface resistance goes to zero when its area is very large.

questions.stem: A flat plate of area 0.5 m$^2$ at 330 K with emissivity 0.85 loses heat to air at 290 K by natural convection with $h=12$ W/m$^2$K and by radiation to large surroundings also at 290 K. Find the total heat loss (convection plus radiation) from one face in W. Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$K$^4$.
questions.explanation: Convection: $q_c=hA\Delta T=12\times0.5\times40=240.0$ W. Radiation: $q_r=\varepsilon A\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)=0.85\times0.5\times5.67\times10^{-8}\times(1.1859e+10-7.0728e+09)=115.3$ W. The total is 355.3 W, with radiation about 32% of the total.
